title: Shemot: holy ground (Exodus 3:5)
hook: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet", for the place is holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: the midrash of Moses chasing a thirsty runaway and carrying it home. Your line was carry the lamb. Did you reach out to someone who drifted? Today, that same shepherd, the same flock, and a bush. Day two hundred twenty-three.

Lots of homes have a rule at the door: shoes off. Some for cleanliness, some out of respect, some because a grandmother said so. Mosques, temples and many homes around the world ask the same thing. There's something about it. The moment you step out of your shoes, you're slower. Quieter. You feel the floor. Moses is out in the wilderness with Jethro's sheep, at a mountain called Horeb, on an ordinary working day. He sees a bush on fire. And the first thing God ever says to him, after his name, is about his shoes.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `SLOWER, QUIETER, THE FLOOR.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: The bush is burning, but it isn't burning up. The text says the bush was not consumed. And Moses says to himself: I'll turn aside and look at this. That's the hinge. The next verse says when God saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him. Moses, Moses. He could have walked on. Plenty of people walk past strange things. He stopped. Then comes today's line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." In Hebrew, admat kodesh. Holy earth. And it's just dirt in the desert, with a thorny bush on it. The rabbis asked why God would speak from a scrubby thorn bush, and not a cedar or a mountaintop. One midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their pain, down in the thorns with them. The holiness isn't in the fancy place. It's where God shows up, and where someone stops to notice. The shoes stayed with the tradition. Priests in the ancient Temple served barefoot. To this day, when the kohanim, the priestly families, rise to bless the congregation, they take off their shoes first. And on Yom Kippur, many Jews set aside leather shoes for the whole day. Shoes are for getting somewhere. Taking them off says: I'm not going anywhere. I'm here. This spot, right now, is enough.
screen: `THE BUSH WAS NOT CONSUMED.` · `HE TURNED ASIDE TO SEE.` · `ADMAT KODESH — HOLY EARTH.` · `PRIESTS BLESS WITHOUT SHOES.` · then, large: `SHOES OFF, IT'S HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and it's literal: take off your shoes and stand still. If you can, do it now. Kick them off, and stand, or sit with your feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground under you. Notice the temperature, the texture. You're not going anywhere for the next two minutes. Let this ordinary spot, this floor in this room, be the place where you stopped and turned aside. The bell holds the time.
Shemot. The portion where Moses turns aside to see a burning bush and is told: take off your shoes, this ground is holy.
Your line: shoes off, it's holy. Tonight, when you take off your shoes, pause for one breath and notice where you're standing. Day two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Before the priestly blessing in synagogue, the kohanim remove their shoes, a custom the Talmud traces to the Temple; on Yom Kippur and Tisha b'Av, many Jews avoid leather shoes all day.

fork.setup: you're a shepherd on an ordinary day. you notice a bush on fire that isn't burning up. what do you do?
options: keep walking; you have sheep to mind.
fork.reveal: Moses said, I will turn aside and see this great sight. only when God saw him turn aside did God call his name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about shoes in sacred places.
what it means: ordinary desert dirt becomes holy where God speaks and someone stops to notice.
what a scholar hears: a midrash asks why God spoke from a thorn bush, and answers: to share the people's suffering.

notes: The thorn-bush midrash (God with Israel in their suffering) cited from memory as Exodus Rabbah 2:5; confirm.
Kohanim removing shoes before the priestly blessing (Sotah 40a, a takkanah of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai) and priests serving barefoot in the Temple; confirm reference.
Horeb as the mountain of the bush is from Exodus 3:1.
